Question: Monic quadratic polynomials \(P(x)\) and \(Q(x)\) have the property that \(P(Q(x))\) has zeros at \(x=-23,\) \(-21,\) \(-17,\) and \(-15,\) and \(Q(P(x))\) has zeros at \(x=-59,\) \(-57,\) \(-51,\) and \(-49.\) What is the sum of the minimum values of \(P(x)\) and \(Q(x)?\)
Solution:
Method 1: Paired roots and symmetry

A monic quadratic can be written as \((x-h)^2+k\). Replacing \(x\) by \(2h-x\) leaves its value unchanged, so it also leaves any polynomial applied to that quadratic unchanged. Thus the zeros of a composition are symmetric about the axis of its inner quadratic.

Both compositions are quartics, so their four listed distinct zeros are their complete zero sets. Reflection exchanges the smallest and largest zeros. Therefore the axes of \(Q\) and \(P\) are, respectively,
\[
\frac{-23-15}{2}=-19,
\qquad
\frac{-59-49}{2}=-54.
\]
Write
\[
Q(x)=(x+19)^2+q,
\qquad
P(x)=(x+54)^2+p,
\]
where \(q\) and \(p\) are their minimum values.

At \(x=-23,-15\), the value of \(Q(x)\) is \(q+16\); at \(x=-21,-17\), it is \(q+4\). These two distinct values must be the two roots of \(P\). Since those roots are symmetric about \(-54\),
\[
\frac{(q+16)+(q+4)}{2}=-54,
\]
which gives \(q=-64\). The roots of \(P\) are consequently \(-48\) and \(-60\). Substituting \(-60\) into its vertex form gives
\[
0=P(-60)=36+p,
\]
so \(p=-36\).

These forms also give
\[
Q(P(x))=
\bigl((x+54)^2-25\bigr)
\bigl((x+54)^2-9\bigr),
\]
whose zeros are exactly \(-59,-57,-51,-49\), as required. Both minimum values are attained when their squared terms are zero. Their sum is
\[
-36-64=\boxed{-100},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{A}\).

Method 2: Compare coefficients of the compositions

The coefficient just below the leading term of a monic polynomial reveals the sum of its roots. Indeed, in a product \(\prod (x-r_i)\), a term of degree one below the leading degree comes from choosing one constant \(-r_i\), so its coefficient is \(-\sum r_i\).

Let
\[
P(x)=x^2+ax+b,
\qquad
Q(x)=x^2+cx+d.
\]
In \(P(Q(x))=Q(x)^2+aQ(x)+b\), the cubic coefficient is \(2c\). The four given roots sum to \(-76\), so \(2c=76\) and \(c=38\). Similarly, the cubic coefficient of \(Q(P(x))\) is \(2a\). Its roots sum to \(-216\), giving \(a=108\).

Complete the square in \(Q\), writing
\[
Q(x)=(x+19)^2+q.
\]
The first set of composition zeros shows that \(q+4\) and \(q+16\) are the two distinct roots of \(P\). Their sum is \(-a=-108\), so
\[
2q+20=-108,
\qquad q=-64.
\]
Thus \(P\) has roots \(-60\) and \(-48\). Because it is monic,
\[
P(x)=(x+60)(x+48)=(x+54)^2-36.
\]
Also, \(Q(x)=(x+19)^2-64\). For the second composition, \(P\) takes the value \(-11\) at \(-59,-49\) and \(-27\) at \(-57,-51\); both values are roots of \(Q\). This verifies the second set of conditions.

Since a real square is nonnegative and can equal zero, the minimum values are \(-36\) and \(-64\). Their sum is \(\boxed{-100}\), choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
